cb_banerjee_morning.text: Good morning, Chief. That's the first time I've said it to your face. It felt strange. I'll be used to it by Thursday.

then.text: About yesterday. You did everything that could be done. Today's a new list, and it's long.
Two more resignation letters on my desk. CarePlus pays better and shouts less.
Pharmacy has put the antibiotic order on hold until Mr. Malhotra finds the money. He's looking under the cushions.
There's a reporter in the lobby again. Waiting times, she says. She's timing the lifts.
The night nurses sent you a cake. I've had it tested. It's just a cake.

cb_banerjee_morning.text: Your intern is in the canteen teaching the canteen staff to wash their hands. She's going to be a terror. I'm so proud.
And there's a name on the admissions board you'll know. Banerjee. Seventy-nine now. She cut her arm on a glass bowl last night and wouldn't come in until morning.
She told the ambulance she'd only see 'the doctor who held my hand'. The crew asked me who that was. I said the Chief.

choose.text: Then the Chief had better go and hold it again.

then.text: Take tissues. She cries at weather forecasts.

choose.text: A kitchen cut. Has anyone asked about her tetanus jabs?

then.text: That's your job, Chief. Ask her. She'll tell you about her husband first. Let her.

cb_banerjee_arrive.text: Beta! Look at you. A white coat with your name stitched on it. In gold!
I dropped my husband's old glass bowl making payesh. Fifty-one years that bowl lasted. One bad evening.
Deep cut on the right forearm, Chief. The bleeding's stopped. There may be glass in it. She won't let me look until you've said hello.
Hello first. Then glass. That's manners.

choose.text: Hello, Mrs. Banerjee. I remember the radio officer who listened to the sea.

then.text: You remember! Nobody remembers anything about old women except their blood pressure.

choose.text: Hello. Let's look at that arm before anything else.

then.text: Straight to work. Same as before. Ask your questions, then.
then.head: nod

then.text: Twenty years since her last tetanus jab. I'll tell theatre. A kitchen bowl isn't a clean knife.

else.text: Nobody asked her about tetanus, Chief. Theatre will want to know.

choose.text: The numbing injection stings for a few seconds. After that, you'll feel pushing, not cutting.

then.text: A few seconds. I had three sons. I can do a few seconds.

choose.text: Not at all. You won't feel a thing.

then.text: Everybody says that. Then they come at you with a needle the size of a pencil.

cb_banerjee_after.text: Minor theatre at two. Tom's laying out the tray.

cb_banerjee_ready.text: I've brought biscuits for the theatre. Marie biscuits. Everyone likes Marie biscuits.
I'm only watching today, Chief. Your patient, your hands, and her biscuits.
Hold my hand while they numb it? Like last time?
cb_banerjee_ready.head: tilt

choose.text: Until the numbing's done. Then I'll need both hands for the stitches.

then.text: Fair. I'll hold the nurse's instead.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I'll hold your hand, and Tom will hold the biscuits.

then.text: Tom will eat the biscuits. I've seen him.
I finished the end of it. The glass was deep. She's fine, Chief. You'll be quicker next time.
The other doctor finished. You held my hand. That's the part I'll remember.

else.text: Finished? I felt the sting, then nothing. Just tugging, like knitting backwards.

cb_banerjee_after_op.text: Now sit. I'll tell you about my grandson in Pune who wants to be a doctor, and you'll tell him not to.

choose.text: Five minutes. Grace is timing me.

then.text: Five minutes is a lot of grandson. I'll talk fast.

choose.text: Not now. But I'll come back on my evening round.

then.text: Evening round. I'll hold you to it. I hold everybody to everything.

hc_night_nurses.text: Chief. Congratulations again. Now, the budget. The strike settlement promised two nurses on every night shift.
That's eleven new salaries. The settlement didn't say where the money comes from. Settlements never do.
It comes from where the money for the new marble in the lobby came from, Mr. Malhotra.

choose.text: We keep the promise. Two on every night shift. Find the money somewhere else.

then.text: Somewhere else. My favourite place. It's very crowded.
Thank you, Chief.
then.head: nod

choose.text: One nurse, and an agency nurse on call for the busy nights.

then.text: Agency nurses don't know where the oxygen is kept. Or the patients' names. But they're cheap.

choose.text: Two nurses. Pay for it from the conference budget. Starting with my trip.

then.text: The Chief cancelling the Chief's own conference. I'll put it in the newsletter.
Singapore will survive without you.

cb_dev_morning.text: Mr. Malhotra rang at five. His son has a pain in his belly. He rang me, then the Dean, then the Dean's wife.
The Dean is retired. The Dean's wife is not amused.
Fifteen, pain that started round the navel and moved low on the right. If that's not an appendix, I'll eat my own clips.
Mr. Malhotra will ask for things. A private room. The Chief in person.

choose.text: Today he's a parent, not the administrator. He gets what every parent gets.

then.text: Every parent gets my tea and my opinions. He'll get both.
then.head: nod

choose.text: He signs my budget. I'll be very careful.

then.text: Careful is good. Careful and fair is better. Remember Kunal Bhatia?

cb_dev_arrive.text: Chief. Thank you for coming down yourself. I know everyone is busy. Dev is... Dev is fifteen.
Papa, stop. You're doing the voice. The budget meeting voice.
It hurts here. Low down, on the right. Since last night. I was sick in Mama's car. Don't tell her it was on the seat.
Temperature thirty-eight. He winces when the trolley bumps. He says the pain moved after midnight.

choose.text: Dev, I'm going to ask you some questions. Your father can stay, but you answer.

then.text: Finally. Someone who talks to me and not about me.

choose.text: Mr. Malhotra, tell me what happened from the start.

then.text: He wasn't even there. He was on a call. About parking.
...About parking.
then.head: down

then.text: Penicillin rash. I'll put it on his band and on the board. Theatre will want a different antibiotic.

else.text: Nobody asked him about allergies, Chief. Theatre will ask.

cb_dev_after.text: It's his appendix, isn't it. Will you do it? You? Not a junior?
cb_dev_after.head: tilt

choose.text: I'll do it, with Dr. Iyer across the table. That's how we do every case, yours or anyone's.

then.text: Every case. Yes. Of course. Every case.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It's the commonest operation we do. He'll be home in two days.

then.text: Two days. We've got a cricket final on Sunday.
You'll be watching it.

cb_dev_after.text: Can Papa stop phoning people now?

hc_dev_room.text: Chief. One small thing. After his operation, the side room. Dev would rest better there. Quieter. Private.
I know Mrs. Chawla is in it. Her chest. But she could go in the bay for one night, surely. With a curtain.
Mrs. Chawla has a resistant chest infection, Mr. Malhotra. That's why she's behind a door.
I've spent twelve years telling doctors who gets which bed. I know exactly what I'm asking. I'm asking anyway. He's my son.

choose.text: Dev stays in the bay, like anyone else. And I'll look in on him myself tonight.

then.text: Like anyone else.
then.head: down

then.text: That's what I'd have told you to say, twelve years ago.

choose.text: Move Mrs. Chawla for one night. Dev gets the side room.

then.text: I'll move her. And I'll write down why, in my handwriting, which is very clear.

choose.text: I'll ask Mrs. Chawla's family. If they say no, it's no.

then.text: They'll say yes. People always say yes to a father. That's the trouble with asking.

cb_dev_ready.text: Will I have a scar? A proper one? For the team photo?
cb_dev_ready.head: tilt

choose.text: A small one, low on the right. About as long as your little finger.

then.text: Little finger. That's nothing. Arjun has a scar from a dog.

choose.text: A small one. Tell them it was a shark.

then.text: A shark. In a swimming pool. They'll believe it. They're very stupid.

cb_dev_ready.text: Chief. I'll be in the corridor. Phone off. I promise.
He won't. He'll put it on silent. Which is worse.

then.text: His appendix was tucked further back than most. I took over at the end. He's fine, Mr. Malhotra.
Fine. Fine is the best word in the language.

else.text: Out, clean, nothing spilled. He'll be eating by tonight.

cb_dev_after_op.text: Did you keep it? The appendix? Can I see?
Chief. I've thanked a lot of doctors in this building. Mostly for coming in under budget. This is different.

choose.text: Sit with him. The budget can wait until tomorrow.

then.text: The budget can wait. Write that down, Dev. You'll never hear me say it again.

choose.text: He did the hard part. He kept still and told me the truth.

then.text: I always tell the truth. Except about the car seat.

cb_tom_morning.text: Morning, Chief. Sit down. You'll want to.

then.text: About yesterday. You did everything that could be done. Today's a new list, and it's long.
Two more resignation letters on my desk. CarePlus pays better and shouts less.

And the board report is at five. Mrs. Rajan wants the numbers by two. She'll have read them by two-oh-one.

cb_tom_morning.text: Tom came in at six to set up theatre. At half past, he was sitting on the floor of the scrub room, very pale, and lying to me.
A lump in his groin that goes back in when he lies down. Since he lifted the new instrument trays last week. Except this morning, it won't go back.
Twenty years he's handed you all scissors. Today somebody hands him a pillow. He'll hate it.

choose.text: Then we'll be gentle. And very, very neat. He'll check.

then.text: He'll count every stitch. Out loud.

choose.text: He's a patient today. He doesn't get to scrub for his own operation.

then.text: Tell him that. Twice. Then lock the scrub room.
then.head: nod

cb_tom_arrive.text: It's nothing, Chief. A pulled muscle. I'll be scrubbed by ten.
It's a lump the size of a lime, Tom. Muscles don't do that.
...It might be slightly more than a pulled muscle.
cb_tom_arrive.head: down

choose.text: Lie back, Tom. For once, I'll do the asking.

then.text: Fine. But if you ask me where the forceps live, I'm answering.

choose.text: Tom, you've counted every swab I've ever used. Let me count something of yours.

then.text: That's the strangest thing anyone's said to me in this building. And I've worked here twenty years.
Two samosas at five, before his shift. Dr. Khan will want that before he goes to sleep.

else.text: Nobody asked when he last ate, Chief. Dr. Khan will ask.

cb_tom_after.text: Who's scrubbing? Not the new boy. The new boy holds scissors like a pen.
cb_tom_after.head: tilt

choose.text: Neha. She learned from you.

then.text: Neha. Good. She'll put everything back where I keep it. And pretend she never moved anything.
then.head: nod

choose.text: You can't scrub for your own operation, Tom. I checked the rules.

then.text: There's no such rule. I looked. Grace wrote one this morning.

cb_tom_after.text: Theatre 2 at two. Neha's already in there, rearranging his trays to annoy him.

cb_tom_ready.text: Before I go to sleep. Count the swabs out loud. I want to hear it, even asleep.
And when Neha says 'all present', make her say it twice.

choose.text: Every swab, out loud, twice. That's your rule.

then.text: Good. Now I can sleep.
then.head: nod

choose.text: We'll count them in your voice. We've all heard it enough.

then.text: Do the voice properly. Deeper. With disappointment.
The sac was stuck down hard. I finished the mesh. He'll heal, Chief. So will you.

else.text: Mesh flat, no gaps. He'll lift trays again in six weeks. Light ones.

choose.text: Twice. Out loud. Neha said 'all present' twice.

then.text: Then I've been operated on properly. Thank you, Chief.

choose.text: We lost a swab. It's fine. It was a small one.

then.text: ...That's not funny.
then.head: up

then.text: That's a little bit funny. Never say it again.

cb_tom_after_op.text: Six weeks. Who hands you the instruments for six weeks?
Neha. She's already moved your clamps.

cb_tom_rota_arrive.text: Four nurses off sick, Chief. The flu's going round the nurses' hostel like gossip.
And with Tom in bed four, that's one more bed and one less pair of hands. Grace says you do tonight's rota with me. She says it's good for you.
It's very good for you. I'll be watching.

then.text: Somebody's got nobody tonight, Chief. I'll stay until midnight and cover them myself. Again.
That holds. Every bed has a name, and nobody's carrying more than they can. I'll sign it.
then.head: nod

else.text: Signed. It'll do. Someone's carrying more than they should, and they'll feel it at four in the morning.

then.text: We can't keep doing this, Chief. We need more nurses, not cleverer rotas.

hc_sponsor.text: Good news, Chief. Medivance Pharma wants to pay for the new day surgery unit. All of it. The building, the beds, the coffee machine.
In return, their name over the door. Their antibiotics first on our list. And their reps in the canteen on Tuesdays. With pens.
Their antibiotic costs three times the old one and works the same. Dr. Khan will have views.

choose.text: Take all of it. A day unit now is worth a few pens.

then.text: Wonderful. I'll order a very large sign.
And I'll order a very large box of the old antibiotic. For the patients.

choose.text: Take the money and the name. Not the list. We prescribe what works.

then.text: They may walk away.
then.head: tilt

then.text: ...They won't. They need the sign more than we need their antibiotic. Probably.

choose.text: No. A hospital that's for sale ends up selling more than its walls.

then.text: That's a lovely sentence. I'll put it on the empty plot where the day unit isn't.

cb_salim_morning.text: Morning, Chief. Quiet so far. Which means it won't be.

then.text: About yesterday. You did everything that could be done. Today's a new list, and it's long.
Two more resignation letters on my desk. CarePlus pays better and shouts less.
Pharmacy has put the antibiotic order on hold until Mr. Malhotra finds the money. He's looking under the cushions.
There's a reporter in the lobby again. Waiting times, she says. She's timing the lifts.
The night nurses sent you a cake. I've had it tested. It's just a cake.
And the board report is at five. Mrs. Rajan wants the numbers by two. She'll have read them by two-oh-one.

cb_salim_morning.text: The ring road's flooded, so every lorry in the state is on the highway through the toll plaza. If anything happens today, it happens there.

choose.text: Then let's check the trauma bay before anything happens.

then.text: Stocked at six. Checked at seven. I'll check it again because you asked nicely.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Then let's hope nothing happens.

then.text: Hope isn't on the stock list, Chief.

cb_salim_triage_arrive.text: A bus lost its brakes at the toll plaza. It went through the queue of motorbikes like skittles.
Six off the first ambulances, more coming. Tag them, Chief. Red now, yellow soon, green walks, black beyond help.

then.text: One you tagged to wait went grey on the trolley, Chief. Dr. Iyer pulled them forward. They'll live. Just.
Every tag right. The trauma bay says it's the calmest crash they've had.
then.head: nod

else.text: Sent in. Dr. Iyer will check the tags again inside. Some of them were generous.

cb_salim_arrive.text: Doctor... it's you. The night doctor. From my bike. Years ago.
cb_salim_arrive.head: tilt

then.text: You stopped the bleeding in my leg. Pooja was seven. She drew you a picture. Purple, with a stethoscope.

else.text: That night, I don't remember much. Intensive care, they told me after. I'm still here. Mostly.

cb_salim_arrive.text: He came off his bike when the bus hit the queue. Left side of his chest and belly into the divider. Pressure ninety and falling.
It hurts here, under the ribs on the left. And my left shoulder. Which is strange. I didn't land on my shoulder.

choose.text: You're in the right place, Salim. A few quick questions.

then.text: Quick. Yes. I'm cold, Doctor. Why am I cold?
then.head: tilt

choose.text: No time for talking. Priya, two big drips and blood.

then.text: Already running, Chief. But ask him things now, while he can still answer.
No allergies. He's sure. I'll tell Dr. Khan.
then.head: nod

else.text: Nobody asked him about allergies. Dr. Khan will be guessing.

cb_salim_after.text: Pressure's eighty-five. Dr. Iyer's opening Theatre 1. She says bring your hands, not your questions.
Call Pooja. She's at school. Tell her... tell her her papa's being difficult.

choose.text: I'll call her myself, the minute you're out.

then.text: The minute. She counts minutes. Like her mother did.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Priya will call her now.

then.text: I'm calling. What do I say?
Say her papa is being difficult. She'll understand.

choose.text: Then Dr. Iyer and I will be doing everything there is. And I'll tell Pooja myself.

then.text: Everything. Good. That's all a man can ask.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It won't go wrong. I won't let it.

then.text: Doctors always say that in films.
The spleen fought us. I finished it. His pressure's a hundred and ten. He'll do.

else.text: Dry. His pressure's a hundred and twenty. Good hands, Chief. Fast hands.

cb_salim_after_op.text: Papa? The nurse said you were being difficult.
Is the doctor there? Can I talk to the doctor?

choose.text: I'm here, Pooja. Your papa's going to be fine. Bring him something to read. He talks too much.

then.text: He does. I'll bring him my maths homework. He hates maths.

choose.text: He's out of the operation and he's stable. You can see him at four.

then.text: Four. I'm counting.

hc_reporter.text: Chief. There's a television van outside. They want the doctor who ran the crash. In front of the trauma bay, looking tired but heroic.
They also want to film inside. The patients. Faces.
Over my dead body. Which they're welcome to film.

choose.text: They can film inside, with written consent from every patient, and nobody who says no.

then.text: Consent from people on morphine. I'll be standing beside every form.

choose.text: No cameras on the ward. I'll speak outside, and thank the nurses by name.

then.text: Outside, by name. Priya will cry. I'll make sure the tissue is in shot.

choose.text: No cameras and no statement. We had a crash, not a show.

then.text: They'll film the van leaving and say 'the hospital declined to comment'. It always sounds like guilt.

cb_mehra_morning.text: Morning, Chief. Board day. I've ironed my second-best apron.

then.text: About yesterday. You did everything that could be done. Today's a new list, and it's long.
Two more resignation letters on my desk. CarePlus pays better and shouts less.
Pharmacy has put the antibiotic order on hold until Mr. Malhotra finds the money. He's looking under the cushions.
There's a reporter in the lobby again. Waiting times, she says. She's timing the lifts.
The night nurses sent you a cake. I've had it tested. It's just a cake.
And the board report is at five. Mrs. Rajan wants the numbers by two. She'll have read them by two-oh-one.

cb_mehra_morning.text: Mrs. Kamala Mehra fell on her own staircase at breakfast. The knee that's clicked for forty years. It's her hip now.
Her son Suresh sits on the board. He's rung Mrs. Rajan, Mr. Malhotra and me. I let it ring.
You met her years ago, when she waited two hours for her heartburn. She remembers. She remembers everything.

then.text: She told the ambulance crew the young doctor had manners. She meant you.
She told the ambulance crew she hoped the young doctor had learned manners. She meant you.

choose.text: She's a patient with a broken hip. That's all she is until it's fixed.

then.text: Tell her son that. Slowly.

choose.text: Board day, and a board member's mother. Of course it is.

then.text: The universe has a sense of humour. It just isn't very good.

cb_mehra_arrive.text: You. The young doctor who made me wait for a bricklayer.

then.text: I told my son you were right. He didn't like it. I enjoyed that.
I wrote to the board about your manners. They wrote back about your skills. Very irritating.

else.text: And now you're the Chief. My son says you're too young. I told him he was too young once.

cb_mehra_arrive.text: Left leg short and turned out, Chief. A broken hip. The pain's controlled. Her son has phoned the desk four times.
Five. He'll phone again. He thinks if he phones enough, things happen faster. Like his father.

choose.text: Then let's give him good news to phone about. A few questions first.

then.text: Questions. Good. Nobody asks old women anything except whether they've fallen.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Mrs. Mehra, I need some answers before we can operate.

then.text: Straight to business. You've changed. Good.
then.head: nod

then.text: Warfarin, for her heart rhythm. Last dose last night. I'll check her clotting and tell Dr. Bhatt.

else.text: Nobody asked about her tablets, Chief. Her handbag rattles.

then.text: And penicillin. Spots, she says, on her wedding day. It's on her band.

cb_mehra_after.text: When? Today? Suresh will want it today. Suresh will want it yesterday.

hc_mehra_first.text: Chief. Two broken hips came in this morning. Mrs. Mehra, and a Mr. Gaikwad, a farmer from Sangli, waiting since yesterday afternoon.
One theatre, one of me, one afternoon. At their age, every day on their back is a day nearer pneumonia.
Suresh Mehra has called the board, the Dean and me. In that order. And today is the board report. I'm only saying.

choose.text: Mr. Gaikwad waited longest. He goes first. Mrs. Mehra second, if Dr. Bhatt will stay late.

then.text: I'll stay. Order the coffee.
then.head: nod

then.text: I'll tell Suresh. From a distance.

choose.text: Mrs. Mehra first. Mr. Gaikwad tomorrow morning.

then.text: Tomorrow morning. I'll tell Mr. Gaikwad's son. He drove all night.
then.head: down

choose.text: Both today. Open Theatre 1 for Mr. Gaikwad, with Dr. Iyer, and pay the overtime.

then.text: Overtime. On a Saturday rate. On board day.
Two hips, two theatres. Like the old days. I love the old days.
Second, after a farmer from Sangli. My son is going to explode. Good. He's never waited for anything in his life.
First. Suresh fixed it. I can see from your face you didn't like it. Neither do I, much.

cb_mehra_ready.text: Will I walk at my grandson's wedding? March. He's marrying a dentist. I have opinions.
cb_mehra_ready.head: tilt

choose.text: If the screw goes in well, you'll stand tomorrow. Walking to March is up to you and the physiotherapist.

then.text: A young man shouting 'one more step'. I'll manage him.

choose.text: You'll dance at it.

then.text: Don't promise dancing. My husband promised dancing. Forty years, not one dance.
The bone was softer than the X-ray said. I finished the plate. It's solid now, Chief.

else.text: Screw dead centre, plate flat. She'll stand tomorrow. Shouting, probably.

cb_mehra_after_op.text: Tell him I'm asleep. Tell him the Chief is very rude and very good. Both. He needs to hear both.

choose.text: I'll tell him the good part. You can tell him the rude part.

then.text: I'll enjoy that.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I'll tell him you're comfortable. That's all I'm allowed to say.

then.text: Comfortable. On a ward. With a screw in my hip. Doctors.

cb_verghese_morning.text: Before you ask: no, I'm fine. It's indigestion. Everybody my age has indigestion.

then.text: About yesterday. You did everything that could be done. Today's a new list, and it's long.
Two more resignation letters on my desk. CarePlus pays better and shouts less.

There's a reporter in the lobby again. Waiting times, she says. She's timing the lifts.
The night nurses sent you a cake. I've had it tested. It's just a cake.
And the board report is at five. Mrs. Rajan wants the numbers by two. She'll have read them by two-oh-one.

cb_verghese_morning.text: I'm holding my clipboard. Against my side. It's a different thing.
Admissions has a CarePlus day case. Keyhole gallbladder three days ago, home the same evening. Fever, yellow, belly like a board.
We've seen this one before, Chief. Mrs. Sinha. Different hospital, same leaflet.

choose.text: Grace, if that indigestion's still there at noon, I'm examining you myself.

then.text: At noon I'll be busy. At one, I'll be busy. I'm always busy, Chief. That's the job.

choose.text: Let's see her. And get her notes from CarePlus before anyone at CarePlus edits them.

then.text: Already asked. They said they'd 'look into it'. That's never a good sentence.

cb_verghese_arrive.text: Are you the Chief? Good. Somebody in charge. CarePlus gave me a leaflet and a number that rings for ever.
Thirty-nine point two, yellow eyes, belly tight as a drum. Operation at CarePlus three days ago.
They said it was textbook. Everybody keeps saying textbook. I count money for a bank, Doctor. When the numbers don't add up, I don't call it textbook.

choose.text: Then let's add up your numbers properly. Tell me everything, from the start.

then.text: From the start. Finally.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I'm sure CarePlus did their best. Let's find out what's going on.

then.text: Their best is why I'm on your trolley.
Penicillin. She swells up. And CarePlus gave it to her anyway, in recovery. She came up in welts. It's on her band now.

else.text: Nobody asked about allergies, Chief. And she's going to theatre.

cb_verghese_after.text: Will you have to go back in through the same holes?
cb_verghese_after.head: tilt

choose.text: The same three holes. We'll wash out the bile and find where it's leaking.

then.text: Find it. And write down what you find. In ink.

choose.text: We'll take a look and see.

then.text: 'Take a look and see.' That's what CarePlus said.

hc_kapoor_back.text: Chief. Congratulations, belatedly. Board votes are so very public.
Mrs. Verghese is ours. We'd like her back. Our ambulance is outside, our surgeon is waiting, our cost entirely. No paperwork.
She's septic, Sameer. She isn't going anywhere in an ambulance today.
Then let's keep it collegial. Whatever you find in there stays between our two hospitals. Surgeons have bad days. Even yours.

then.text: After all, you kept Mrs. Sinha's leak in the family. I'm only asking for the same courtesy.

choose.text: She stays. What I find goes to her, in writing, and to the medical council.

then.text: The council. How formal. My lawyers love formal.

choose.text: She stays. I'll tell her what I find. And I'll ring you first, surgeon to surgeon, before anything's written.

then.text: Surgeon to surgeon. That's all I ask. I'll wait for your call.

They're in the corridor. One of them is drawing my appendix. He's never seen one. Neither have I.

choose.text: Forget the exam for today. Let me find out what's wrong first.

then.text: Forget the exam. My father will need to hear that from you personally.

choose.text: Tell your friend the appendix is the shape of a small worm. He can fix the drawing.

then.text: A worm. He's drawn it like a banana. I'll tell him. He'll be devastated.
Penicillin allergy. Swollen lips at school. I'll put it on his band in red, and on the theatre board.

else.text: Nobody asked him about allergies, Chief. Theatre will give the usual antibiotic unless somebody tells them.

cb_arif_after.text: Do I need an operation? Honestly? My mother will want to know everything. She's a pharmacist.
cb_arif_after.head: tilt

choose.text: Yes. Your appendix is inflamed, and it comes out today, before it bursts.

then.text: Today. Okay. Okay. I'll ring her. You'll talk to her? She'll have questions. Forty of them.

choose.text: Probably. Let's get you comfortable first, and I'll explain it all to you and your mother.

then.text: Probably. That's a doctor's yes, isn't it. My mother says 'probably' the same way.

cb_arif_after.text: Theatre 2 at two. I'll keep the friends out. They've started a group chat about it.

cb_arif_ready.text: My mother rang Dr. Khan. Dr. Khan is still on the phone. I'm sorry.
She's very well informed. She's asked for my qualifications. I've sent them.

choose.text: You're in very good hands, Arif. Dr. Khan has put thousands of people to sleep. And woken them up.

then.text: Woken them up. That's the important part. Please tell my mother that part.
then.head: nod

choose.text: When you wake up, it'll be lunchtime, and the exam will be somebody else's problem.

then.text: Somebody else's problem. That's the nicest thing anyone's said to me this term.
It had stuck itself to everything. I finished it. He'll be fine, Chief. Tired, and fine.

else.text: Out, before it burst. Neat work. He'll be home in two days, and back at his desk complaining in three.

cb_arif_after_op.text: Is it out? Can I see it? My friends want a photograph. For science.
cb_arif_after_op.head: tilt

choose.text: It's in a jar. One photograph. For science.

then.text: For science. They'll put it on the hostel noticeboard. You'll be famous.

choose.text: Sleep first. Science can wait until tomorrow.

then.text: Science can wait. You sound like my mother. She'll like you.
then.head: nod

cb_mohan_arrive.text: Doctor sahib, it's nothing. A small lump. I'll push it back and go. Forty cylinders on the tempo.
He's the man who brings our gas cylinders, Chief. A lump in his groin that's been stuck since he lifted one this morning. It's hard, and he's grey.
I'm not grey. I'm always this colour. It's the stairs.
cb_mohan_arrive.head: down

choose.text: Lie back, Mr. Tiwari. The cylinders can wait an hour. You can't.

then.text: An hour. The canteen won't be able to make chai. You're a brave man, doctor.

choose.text: Don't push it back. If it's stuck, it stays where it is until I've looked.

then.text: Don't push. Okay. You're the doctor. I'm only the cylinders.
then.head: nod

then.text: A big plate of poha at five. Dr. Khan will want that before anything else.

else.text: Nobody asked when he last ate, Chief. Dr. Khan will ask. Loudly.

cb_mohan_after.text: My daughter is at the nursing college. She'll want to know what you're doing. Tell me properly, so I can tell her.
cb_mohan_after.head: tilt

choose.text: Your bowel has slipped through a weak spot and got stuck. We free it, check it's healthy, and patch the spot with mesh.

then.text: Mesh. Like a sieve. My wife will understand that. She sieves everything.

choose.text: A small operation today, so it doesn't happen again.

then.text: Small. My daughter will say nothing is small. She's very strict.

cb_mohan_after.text: Theatre 2 at two. His driver's parked in the ambulance bay. I've asked him nicely. Twice.

cb_mohan_ready.text: Doctor, who will deliver the cylinders this week? The canteen needs two. Theatre needs one.
I'll ring the depot. Theatre's oxygen comes from a different man. Don't worry about our gas.

choose.text: I'll make sure the canteen gets its cylinders. You think about getting better.

then.text: You'll make sure. The Chief, delivering cylinders. I'll tell everyone.

choose.text: If the canteen runs out of chai, I'll blame you personally.

then.text: Blame me. Everybody does. When the gas runs out, nobody blames the gas.
The loop was tight and angry. I finished the mesh. He'll heal, Chief.

else.text: The bowel pinked up nicely, and the mesh is flat. He'll be carrying again in six weeks. Lighter loads, if he listens.

cb_mohan_after_op.text: Six weeks? Who carries the cylinders for six weeks?

choose.text: I'll write to your depot myself. Six weeks of light work, on full pay.

then.text: On a Chief's letter. My supervisor will frame it. Then he'll argue with it.

choose.text: Somebody else. If you lift too soon, it'll come back.

then.text: Somebody else. Okay. I'll supervise. From a chair.
then.head: nod

cb_savitri_arrive.text: Doctor! I brought tea. For the nurses. You also, if you're not too important.
Sixty-six, runs the tea stall at the bus stand. A glass broke in her hand while she was washing up. Deep cut across the left palm. The towel's doing its best.
Thirty-one years, never a cut. Today, one glass. The old kind. Thick.

choose.text: Thank you for the tea. Now let me look after the hand that made it.

then.text: Such a nice doctor. You'll come to the stall. Twelve rupees for you. Ten, now.

choose.text: Let's see that hand before anything else.

then.text: Straight to work. Good. My customers are waiting.
then.head: nod

then.text: Twenty years since her last tetanus jab. Broken glass at a bus stand isn't clean. I'll tell theatre.

else.text: Nobody asked about tetanus, Chief. A wound from a bus stand needs somebody to ask.

cb_savitri_after.text: Will I be able to hold a kettle? I have to hold a kettle. That's the whole job.
cb_savitri_after.head: tilt

choose.text: In about ten days, if we find every bit of glass and it heals clean.

then.text: Ten days. My nephew will run the stall. He'll make terrible tea. People will miss me.

choose.text: Of course. You'll be back tomorrow.

then.text: Tomorrow? With a hand like this? Doctor, I'm old, not foolish.

cb_savitri_after.text: Minor theatre at two. Tom's laying out the tray. He's already had two cups.

cb_savitri_ready.text: Will the injection hurt? I can stand anything except injections. And the price of milk.
cb_savitri_ready.head: tilt

cb_savitri_ready.text: I'm only watching, Chief. Your patient, your hands, and her tea.

choose.text: It stings for a few seconds. After that, you'll feel pushing, not cutting.

then.text: A few seconds. I can do a few seconds. I've done thirty-one years.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Tell me about the bus drivers while I numb it. Which one's the worst?

then.text: The worst? The forty-two's driver. Never pays. Says he'll pay Friday. Friday never comes.
The glass was deep. I finished the end of it. She'll heal, Chief.

else.text: Every sliver out, and neat stitches. She'll be pouring tea in ten days.

cb_savitri_after_op.text: Finished? I felt only tugging. Like somebody darning a sock.

choose.text: Keep it dry, keep it up, and come back in five days so I can look.

then.text: Dry, up, five days. I'll bring tea when I come. Don't argue.

choose.text: No washing glasses for ten days. Your nephew can learn.

then.text: My nephew. He'll break every glass at the stall. You'll see him next week.

cb_usha_arrive.text: Good morning. Sit up straight, Priya. Yes, I remember you. Third row, by the window. Always late.
Yes, Ma'am. Sixty-one, Chief. Pain under the right ribs since her niece's engagement dinner, and a fever since midnight. She was my headmistress.
And now I'm a patient. Very strange. Usually I'm the one asking the questions.

choose.text: Then today I'll ask, and you can mark my questions, Mrs. Krishnan.

then.text: Good. I'll be fair. I was always fair. Ask Priya.

choose.text: Let's start with the pain, and leave school out of it.

then.text: Straight to the point. Good. Too many people waste the first five minutes.
then.head: nod

then.text: Aspirin every morning for her heart, and she took it at seven. Theatre will keep blood ready. Nobody stops a heart aspirin without asking.

else.text: Nobody asked about blood thinners, Chief. At her age, with a heart, somebody should.

cb_usha_after.text: Is it the gallbladder? Speak clearly. I can't bear mumbling.
cb_usha_after.head: tilt

choose.text: Yes. Stones, and the gallbladder is inflamed now. It comes out today, by keyhole.

then.text: Clear and correct. Ten out of ten. Don't let it go to your head.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It looks like your gallbladder. We'll talk about the next steps soon.

then.text: Soon. Six out of ten. Be more precise next time.

cb_usha_after.text: Theatre 2 at two. Neha's terrified. She was in Mrs. Krishnan's class too.

cb_usha_ready.text: Neha Joshi. I remember you. Your handwriting was dreadful. Is it better now?
Yes, Ma'am. I write the theatre count. Everybody can read it.
cb_usha_ready.head: nod

choose.text: She's the best scrub nurse we have, Mrs. Krishnan. You taught her well.

then.text: I taught her to sit still. The rest she did herself.

choose.text: If her handwriting slips, you can give her a detention after.

then.text: A detention. I'd forgotten how much I enjoyed those.
The liver bed oozed. I finished it. She's fine, Chief.

else.text: Out by keyhole, stones and all. Four little scars. She'll inspect them.

choose.text: It's out. Four small cuts, no stones left, and you'll go home in two days.

then.text: Clear. Concise. Nine out of ten. Nobody gets ten.
then.head: nod

choose.text: All done. Rest now, and we'll talk when you're awake.

then.text: I am awake. But fine. Seven out of ten. Go away.

cb_rosy_arrive.text: Young doctor. Before anything: somebody must feed Clementine. Half a tin at noon, half at six. She won't eat the cheap one.
Eighty-three, fell over her cat at six this morning. Lay on the floor until the milkman found her. Her left leg is short and turned out.
Clementine is not to blame. She has slept on that step for nine years. I'm the one who changed.

choose.text: We'll find somebody to feed Clementine. Now let me look after you.

then.text: Thank you. The tin opener is in the second drawer. It sticks.

choose.text: The cat can wait an hour, Mrs. Pereira. Your hip can't.

then.text: You've never met Clementine. But fine. Ask.
Warfarin for her heart, last dose last night, and I gave the vitamin K at breakfast. Dr. Bhatt will want her clotting before he lets anyone cut.

else.text: Nobody asked about her medicines, Chief. At eighty-three, with an irregular heart, somebody should.

then.text: And penicillin, since 1971. She finished the Chopin first. I've put it on the board.

cb_rosy_after.text: Will I play again? I don't play with my hip, but I need it to get to the piano.
cb_rosy_after.head: tilt

choose.text: With a screw and a plate, you'll be walking with a frame in days, and to the piano in weeks.

then.text: Weeks. My last pupil has a recital in March. I'll be there. On a frame, if necessary.

choose.text: You'll be back at the piano in no time.

then.text: No time. Doctors always say no time. Time is the only thing I have plenty of.

cb_rosy_after.text: Theatre 3 at two. I'll feed the cat on my way home. Half a tin. The good one.

cb_rosy_ready.text: Dr. Bhatt says I'll be awake behind a screen. May we have music? Something with a steady tempo.
I've found some Chopin on my phone. Nocturnes. Tom says they're too sad for theatre.

choose.text: Chopin it is. Steady tempo, steady hands.

then.text: Steady tempo, steady hands. You'd have made a pianist. A poor one, but a pianist.

choose.text: Something fast, please. Dr. Bhatt works to the beat.

then.text: Then no Chopin. He'd rush. Everybody rushes Chopin.
Old bone, and it fought me. I finished the screws. It'll hold, Chief.

else.text: Lined up, screw dead centre, plate flat. She hummed the whole way through. In tune.

cb_rosy_after_op.text: Is it done? I heard you counting. You count well. Most people rush.
cb_rosy_after_op.head: tilt

choose.text: It's done. Priya is feeding Clementine tonight. The good tin.

then.text: The good tin. Then I can sleep. Thank you, young doctor.

choose.text: It's done. The physio will have you standing tomorrow.

then.text: Tomorrow. Scales at seven, then. Walking scales.
then.head: nod

cb_gurdeep_arrive.text: Doctor. I walked in. That's good, yes? A man who walks in can't be too bad.
Forty-five. His lorry rolled at the top of the ghat. The steering wheel hit him under the left ribs. Pressure's ninety-five and falling. He's pale and sweating.
Eighteen tonnes of onions on the road. The village is collecting them. Somebody should tell my company.

choose.text: Your company can wait. Lie still, and tell me exactly where it hurts.

then.text: Still. Okay. I've been still for twenty-five years in that cab. I can do still.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Walking in doesn't mean it isn't bad. We need to move fast.

then.text: Fast. Good. I don't like the way this feels.
then.head: down

then.text: Pain in his left shoulder tip, with a blow under the left ribs. That's blood under his diaphragm. I'll ring theatre now.

else.text: Nobody asked where else it hurts, Chief. His pressure's still dropping. Theatre needs to know what we think it is.

cb_gurdeep_after.text: Is it bad, doctor? Tell me straight. I drive the ghat. I like things straight.
cb_gurdeep_after.head: tilt

choose.text: Your spleen is probably bleeding. We need to operate now, before you lose much more.

then.text: Now. Straight. Thank you. Ring my brother. He's driving from Nashik.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Something inside is bleeding. We're going to fix it.

then.text: Fix it. Okay. I trust you. I've no choice, but I trust you.

cb_gurdeep_after.text: Theatre 1 is open. Dr. Iyer's scrubbing. Blood's on its way down.

cb_gurdeep_ready.text: Doctor, if something happens, my brother has the lorry papers. And the onion money. Tell him.
Nothing's happening except sleep. Count backwards from ten for me.
cb_gurdeep_ready.head: nod

choose.text: I'll tell him myself. And I'll tell him you were brave.

then.text: Brave. He won't believe it. Ten, nine, eight...
then.head: nod

choose.text: Nothing will happen. We've done this many times.

then.text: Many times. Good. Ten, nine...
then.head: nod

then.text: It bled hard. I finished it. He's alive, Chief, and his pressure's holding.

else.text: Spleen out, belly dry, nothing else broken. You moved fast. That's what saved him.

cb_gurdeep_after_op.text: Doctor. My brother came? Did he bring the onions back?
cb_gurdeep_after_op.head: tilt

choose.text: He's here. He's been in the corridor for two hours. No onions.

then.text: No onions. Typical. Send him in.

choose.text: No spleen means vaccines before you go home, and antibiotics for any fever. I'll explain it all.

then.text: Vaccines. Like a child. Fine. You saved my life. I'll take the vaccines.
then.head: nod

cb_anwar_arrive.text: Assalamu alaikum, doctor. Excuse the cough. It's older than you.
Sixty-seven, retired tailor. A lump in his left groin that's been stuck since he coughed at dawn. It's tight, and tender. And he hasn't passed wind.
Forty years of beedis, my son says. He's right. Don't tell him I said so.

choose.text: Walaikum assalam, Mr. Hussain. Let's see what that cough has done.

then.text: Such good manners. Your mother raised you well.

choose.text: Lie back, and try not to cough while I look.

then.text: Try not to cough. I've been trying for forty years.
A paratha at five, after prayers. A big one. Dr. Khan will want to know.

else.text: Nobody asked when he last ate, Chief. Dr. Khan will.

cb_anwar_after.text: Will the cough break your stitches? Tell me honestly. I'm a tailor. I know about stitches.
cb_anwar_after.head: tilt

choose.text: It could, so we'll use mesh, strong and flat. And you hold a pillow on it when you cough.

then.text: A pillow. Like pressing a seam before you sew. Sensible.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Don't worry about the stitches. They'll hold.

then.text: Every apprentice says that. Then the seam splits at the wedding.

cb_anwar_after.text: Theatre 2 at two. Neha's scrubbing. He's asked to inspect her knots.

cb_anwar_ready.text: Young lady. Your stitches. Small and even, yes? Like a good suit.
Small and even, Mr. Hussain. I promise. The Chief does the stitching.
cb_anwar_ready.head: nod

choose.text: Small, even, and strong enough for that cough.

then.text: Strong enough for my cough. That's a big promise. I accept.

choose.text: If you don't like the seam, you can take it in yourself.

then.text: Take it in. At my age. I'll let it out instead. More biryani.
The loop was tight. I finished the repair. It'll hold, Chief.

else.text: Bowel's pink, mesh is flat, and the stitches are very even. He'll check.

cb_anwar_after_op.text: Show me the seam. ...Hm. Good seam. Small. Even. Who taught you?
cb_anwar_after_op.head: tilt

choose.text: A lot of patient people. Now you're one of them.

then.text: Patient people. Yes. That's how you learn anything.

choose.text: Hold the pillow when you cough, and no lifting for six weeks.

then.text: Pillow. No lifting. My daughter-in-law will be delighted. She's wanted me to sit down for years.

cb_kavita_arrive.text: Ticket? No, sorry. Habit. Doctor, I've got pain here and a son who won't look up from his phone.
Forty-four, bus conductor on the forty-two. Pain under the right ribs since her night shift, shivering since four. She came in on her own bus.
The driver didn't charge me. First time in eleven years. I knew it was serious.

choose.text: Let's make the free ride worth it. Tell me about the pain.

then.text: Worth it. I like that. Okay. Ask.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Lie back. Questions first, then we'll see.

then.text: Questions. Fine. I ask questions all night. 'Where to?' 'Change?'
Two aspirin at six, for what she thought was acidity. Theatre will keep blood ready.

else.text: Nobody asked what she's taken, Chief. People take all sorts before they come in.

cb_kavita_after.text: Was it the vada pav? Tell me it wasn't the vada pav. I can't give up vada pav.
cb_kavita_after.head: tilt

choose.text: Stones in your gallbladder, months in the making. The vada pav only rang the bell.

then.text: Only rang the bell. Like a passenger. I can live with that.

choose.text: Fried food makes it worse. Less of it, after this.

then.text: Less vada pav. You're a cruel person, doctor.

cb_kavita_after.text: Theatre 2 at two. Her son's asked for the wi-fi password. I've said no.

cb_kavita_ready.text: How long will it take? The forty-two does the round trip in fifty minutes.
cb_kavita_ready.head: tilt

cb_kavita_ready.text: We're slower than the forty-two. But we stop at every stop, and nobody falls off.

choose.text: About an hour. Your son will see you when you wake up.

then.text: An hour. Tell him to look up from his phone when I come out. Once.
then.head: nod

choose.text: About ten minutes longer than the forty-two. No tickets needed.

then.text: No tickets. Best ride I'll ever get.
The liver bed oozed. I finished it. She's fine, Chief.

else.text: Out by keyhole. Four little scars. She asked if she could keep the stones for her ticket machine.

cb_kavita_after_op.text: Is my son here? Is he on his phone?
cb_kavita_after_op.head: tilt

choose.text: He's here. He put the phone away when they wheeled you out. He's been holding your ticket machine.

then.text: He put it away? Then I really was ill.

choose.text: Home in two days. Light work for two weeks. No night shifts.

then.text: No night shifts. The depot will have to find someone. They'll hate it. Good.
Half the night shift is stuck behind the flooded underpass, Chief. One of them rang from a rickshaw floating past the post office.
The rain's taken out the road from the nurses' hostel. Three can't get in. One swam. Don't tell Grace.
Two off with fever, two stuck at home with water in the kitchen. Rota, Chief, and quickly.

monsoon_rota_arrive.text: Every bed needs a name before eight. The rain doesn't care.

then.text: A bus aquaplaned into a lorry on the highway. The rain's so heavy the ambulances can't see the road.
A pile-up under the flyover. Six vehicles. The water was up to the wheels and nobody slowed down.
The ghat road again. A landslide in front of a bus, and a line of bikes behind it.

monsoon_triage_arrive.text: They're soaked and cold, and cold hides shock. Red now, yellow soon, green walks, black beyond help. Tag them, Chief.

then.text: Half the nurses are on festival leave, Chief. The other half want to be. Rota.
Two of the regulars are at their villages, one's at her sister's wedding, and the agency is charging festival rates. Rota, Chief.
Three nurses on leave, two who ate the canteen's festival sweets and regret it. Rota, Chief.

festival_rota_arrive.text: Every bed needs a name before eight. Then I'm going to see the fireworks. From the window.

then.text: The festival grounds, Chief. A firework stall went up, and the crowd ran into the stage. The stage fell.
A crush at the festival gate. Too many people, one gate, and a firework somebody let off to make them hurry.
The lighting tower at the festival came down in the wind. Then the firework stall caught. Everybody's coming here.

festival_triage_arrive.text: Burns, crushes, and a lot of shouting. The loud ones aren't the sick ones. Tag them, Chief.

then.text: One you tagged to wait went grey on the trolley, Chief. Dr. Iyer pulled them forward. They'll live. Just.
Every tag right. The burns unit says it's the best-sorted festival they've ever had. They've had a lot.
then.head: nod

else.text: Sent in. Dr. Iyer will check the tags again inside. One or two were hopeful.

then.text: The stomach bug's taken two more nurses, Chief. Lata's on the bathroom floor at home, phoning in her apologies.
Six new admissions with the bug overnight, and three of our nurses with it too. The water's still bad in the old town.
Neha's on loan from theatre. The list's cancelled, because half the anaesthetists have the bug.

outbreak_rota_arrive.text: The rule that matters this week: the bug never shares a nurse with anyone who can't fight it. Every bed needs a name by eight.

then.text: Somebody's got nobody tonight, Chief. In an outbreak. I'll stay and cover them myself.
That holds. The bug stays on one side of the floor, and the fragile ones stay on the other. I'll sign it.
then.head: nod

else.text: Signed. It'll do. But somebody's hands go from the bug to someone who can't fight it, and that worries me.

then.text: We can't keep doing this, Chief. We need more nurses, not cleverer rotas.

outbreak_triage_arrive.text: The bug's in every other bed, Chief, and now the highway's sent a bus crash. They don't take turns.
Red now, yellow soon, green walks, black beyond help. Tag them, and wash your hands after.

board_report.text: Chief. Sit, please. The board has your numbers: staff, money, and what the town thinks of us. Mr. Malhotra has made a chart.
Three bars. I chose the colours myself.

then.text: Your first report. I was a judge for nineteen years. First reports tell you less than people think, and more than they'd like.
Strong. The nurses are staying, the money adds up, and the town trusts us with its relatives. I'll keep this one.
then.head: nod

then.text: Even the money bar is green. I've never had a green money bar. I may frame it.
Poor. I won't decorate it.
Nurses are leaving. A hospital without nurses is an expensive car park.
The money doesn't add up. Mr. Malhotra has stopped sleeping.
And the town is losing faith. The newspaper has a weekly column about our waiting times. It's very well written.
This is the second poor report running. Dr. Kapoor has offered CarePlus 'management support'. Some of the board would like to accept.

else.text: One poor report is a warning. Two is a pattern. Boards act on patterns.
Mixed. Some of it is good. Some of it will be a problem by the next report.

then.text: Nurses are leaving. A hospital without nurses is an expensive car park.
The money doesn't add up. Mr. Malhotra has stopped sleeping.
And the town is losing faith. The newspaper has a weekly column about our waiting times. It's very well written.
And remember, the bar is higher than it was. The town keeps growing. So do our expectations.
The bar is higher this year, Chief. Last year's good is this year's ordinary.
We expect more every year. That isn't unkindness. That's a growing town.

board_report.text: What will you do before the next report?
board_report.head: tilt

choose.text: Look after the staff first. Everything in this building stands on them.

then.text: Noted. Mr. Malhotra, stop wincing.

choose.text: Get the money right. Nothing lasts if we can't pay for it.

then.text: Music. To my ears.

choose.text: Earn the town's trust. Shorter waits, open doors, and the truth when we get it wrong.

then.text: The truth when you get it wrong. That's the part people forget to budget for.
then.head: nod

board_report.text: We'll meet again on the next board day. Good evening, Chief.
